doc.title: David Finck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, May 29, 2015

title: Learning Latin bass in Paquito D'Rivera's band
summary: Finck describes five years with Paquito D'Rivera, recommended by Claudio Roditi, and learning Latin and samba bass lines on the spot.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: I really love this. How did you learn how to play that music?

Let me tell you something. That record is one of the records of which I am most proud. And I played in Paquito D’Rivera’s band I guess probably about five years. And I was recommended to Paquito by Claudio Roditi who is a wonderful trumpet player, Brazilian guy, who I guess heard that I had some kind of sense of this music. I always liked it. Like even in high school I remember I’d turn on the salsa station and go man that’s cool. And the bass players totally function — like there’s another example of functioning as the bass of the rhythm and harmony, and you have to maintain — there are some rules about playing Latin music to which you must adhere, which, us gringos do the best we can. Because I didn’t grow up with it. But what happened was both Paquito and Claudio, who are very open and helpful, we’d be playing and I remember Paquito coming over and singing in my ear a cha-cha-cha bass line. A very traditional one. And I played and, “oh no, no, no, no, no, no.” And then I’d get it. And so that was like on-the-spot training. And Claudio did the same thing with samba. He might sing a little rhythm or a little line that was traditional samba rhythm that I could incorporate. That helped a lot. In Paquito’s
band we also had a drummer who was very strong with that stuff, and a pianist — I think that’s Danilo Perez on that.

So that became — I became a student with those guys. I don’t even know if I could do that now. I was pretty good at it then and it’s a different mindset. And now when I listen to a really great Latin jazz bass player like Andy Gonzalez and I hear him play, and I go there’s an accent that he’s got that I don’t have. And a dear friend of mine made me a copy of a beautiful record. Talk about stealing stuff and making illegal copies — but he wanted me to hear this record and he was on it. And it was an Eddie Palmieri record. And he said, “listen to the bass player.” And the bass player played a little behind. He played — you know in a bass line theoretically you’d be going [scats]. That’s how I play it. He played [scats]. He had the six going on with the four and he was completely loose with it. And when you — I guess insert that into the machinery of the rest of the rhythm section it feels unbelievable. And I tried to do it. I played along with the record. I kind of got it but it’s like speaking another language.
